planting.note: Sow 4-8 weeks before first frost for a fall and winter crop, or as soon as soil can be worked in earliest spring; this French heirloom is prized for bearing frost and freezes better than many other mâche types.

directions: Sow seed shallowly and thinly into cool, moist soil, since germination slows dramatically once soil warms past the mid-60s. D'Etampes is an old French heirloom mâche with dark green, spoon-shaped leaves that stand up to hard freezes and light snow better than most other named selections, making it a reliable choice for winter harvest under row cover or cold frame. The rosettes have the classic mild, nutty flavor typical of mâche and are ready to cut whole or picked leaf by leaf. Succession sow into early fall for a continuous supply through the coldest months.

planting.note: In cold-winter regions sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop or as early as soil can be worked in spring; in mild-winter regions sow in late summer or early fall to overwinter for a spring harvest.

directions: Sow seed about 1/4 inch deep and keep the bed consistently moist and weeded, since Gala develops slowly and germinates over a long, uneven window even in ideal cool conditions. This heirloom French selection is valued for good mildew resistance and a rich, buttery texture, forming neat, fist-sized rosettes of oval leaves with a mild, nutty flavor. It tolerates light frost well and holds in the garden through cold snaps better than many quick-maturing salad greens. Harvest whole rosettes by cutting them at the base once they reach full size.

planting.note: Direct sow successionally from early spring through midsummer in full sun for a continuous supply of tender leaves, or sow in late summer for a winter harvest in mild climates; unlike common mâche this species tolerates warm weather without bolting as quickly.

directions: Direct sow into fairly rich, well-drained soil in a sunny spot; unlike Valerianella locusta, this southern European species cannot be grown in shade and needs open sun to perform well. Italian corn salad is distinguished from common mâche by its softly hairy leaves and fruit and its greater tolerance of warm weather, making it a traditional choice in Italy and southern France where it does not run to seed as quickly as common corn salad during a hot spell. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than Valerianella locusta, so late sowings benefit from a sheltered site or row cover in colder gardens. Keep soil evenly moist, since drought stress hastens bolting and increases bitterness in the small, pale-blue-flowered rosettes.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall to keep the cultivar true-to-type, since plants grown from seed frequently revert toward solid green; set divisions into moist, humus-rich soil in sun to partial shade.

directions: Grow in ordinary, moisture-retentive garden soil in full sun to partial shade; this ornamental sport of yellow rocket forms low, slow-spreading rosettes of lyre-shaped, dark green leaves marbled with cream and pale yellow, making it a bright edging plant for borders and cottage gardens through fall, winter, and spring. Small four-petaled yellow flowers appear on branching stems in spring above the variegated foliage, followed by self-sown seedlings that may not retain the parent's coloring. Like the straight species, the young leaves carry a peppery, watercress-like bite and are edible in small amounts, though this form is grown chiefly for its foliage display. Trim off any all-green reverted shoots promptly to keep the clump uniformly variegated.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or early spring into gritty, fast-draining but consistently moist soil tucked among rocks or at the edge of a partially shaded bed; established plants also spread readily from small offset divisions.

directions: Native from Alaska south to California along moist, rocky slopes, cliffs, and creek banks, littleleaf miner's lettuce is a low, stoloniferous perennial forming rosettes of small, fleshy, spoon-shaped leaves topped by loose sprays of pink or white five-petaled flowers in spring and summer. It spreads by trailing stolons tipped with tiny rooting plantlets, gradually knitting together a groundcover mat well suited to a partially shaded rock garden, stone wall, or gravelly bed with reliable moisture. Like its relatives, the mild, slightly succulent leaves are edible raw in salads. This is a distinct, longer-lived perennial species, not to be confused with the annual Claytonia perfoliata, which is sometimes still sold under the older name Montia perfoliata.

planting.note: Direct sow every 2 weeks from early spring through fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Uber combines the fast, uniform growth of standard salad arugula with the deeply lobed, wild-arugula-style leaf shape favored by chefs.

directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed shallowly (about 1/8 inch deep) into cool, moist soil for quick, even germination. Uber produces fast-growing, deeply lobed leaves that give it the refined look of wild arugula while keeping the speed and uniformity of a standard salad-type strain, with a mild, nutty, peppery flavor. It performs especially well as a winter crop in high tunnels or cool greenhouses and tolerates cold better than many salad arugulas. Cut leaves about an inch above the soil line for quick regrowth, and cover new plantings with floating row cover to keep flea beetles off young seedlings.
